title: Suppression of a leaf-inhabiting thrips is temporarily reduced, but eventually enhanced by the presence of a flower-inhabiting thrips
content:
Abstract
When herbivore species share natural enemies, indirect predator-mediated interactions between herbivores may arise, with outcomes ranging from positive to negative depending on time scale, prey distribution, and predator traits. We evaluated such interactions between 2 thrips species (Thysanoptera: Thripidae) occupying distinct plant parts on gerbera: the flower thrips Frankliniella occidentalis (Pergande) and the leaf-inhabiting thrips Echinothrips americanus Morgan, both attacked by the omnivorous predators Orius laevigatus (Fieber) and Orius majusculus (Reuter) (Hemiptera: Anthocoridae). On leaf-disc arenas, both predators consumed more of the less mobile E. americanus than of F. occidentalis. On whole plants, however, the presence of F. occidentalis was associated with a short-term positive effect on densities of E. americanus, irrespective of predator species. This effect was reversed in the longer term, and E. americanus densities were lower in the presence of F. occidentalis. Furthermore, the 2 predators differed in their effects: O. laevigatus persisted at higher densities and suppressed F. occidentalis more than O. majusculus, whereas O. majusculus suppressed E. americanus more in the short term but persisted less well than O. laevigatus. Gerbera flowers sustained oviposition of O. laevigatus, but not of O. majusculus, even without animal prey, which may explain their contrasting persistence. These results suggest that effects of predator-mediated interactions between herbivores can shift from positive to negative through time. We discuss the importance of within-plant prey distribution, predator persistence, and plant-provided foods in shaping interactions mediated by omnivorous predators.
